Standing waves on a string fixed at both ends

⚠ Figure failed to load

plan.contextChunk: This figure stacks five drawings of the same fixed string. At the top a horizontal line runs between two black endpoint dots, each labeled "Node", with a double-headed dimension arrow above it labeled L. Beneath come four standing-wave patterns on lines of that same length, labeled at the left n = 1, n = 2, n = 3, and n = 4. Each is a dark blue curve with a pale mirror-image curve, the two outlining the envelope the string sweeps, ends pinned and interior crossing points rising from none to three. Two expressions sit to the right of each: 1/2 lambda_1 = L and lambda_1 = 2/1 L, then lambda_2 = L and lambda_2 = 2/2 L, then 3/2 lambda_3 = L and lambda_3 = 2/3 L, then 4/2 lambda_4 = L and lambda_4 = 2/4 L. A general statement closes the lower right, lambda_n = 2/n L for n = 1, 2, 3, and so on. Holding one length fixed while packing in more half-wavelengths shows how the pinned ends restrict which wavelengths fit. The sequence introduces the normal modes of a string fixed at both ends.

interactionPlan.concept: A string fixed at both ends can only support standing waves whose half-wavelengths fit a whole number of times into the string length, giving the normal modes lambda_n = 2L/n.
elements: Top reference line: horizontal straight line of length L between two filled black endpoint dots
Double-headed dimension arrow above the top line with vertical end ticks, labeled 'L'
Labels 'Node' beneath each endpoint dot of the top reference line
Four stacked standing-wave panels on lines of identical length L, one per mode
Left-hand mode labels: 'n = 1', 'n = 2', 'n = 3', 'n = 4'
Dark blue sinusoidal curve in each panel (instantaneous string shape)
Pale blue mirror-image curve in each panel (opposite phase, outlining the oscillation envelope)
Filled black dots marking the pinned endpoints of every wave panel
Interior crossing points (nodes): 0 for n=1, 1 for n=2, 2 for n=3, 3 for n=4
Right-hand fit equations: '1/2 lambda_1 = L', 'lambda_2 = L', '3/2 lambda_3 = L', '4/2 lambda_4 = L'
Right-hand wavelength results: 'lambda_1 = 2/1 L', 'lambda_2 = 2/2 L', 'lambda_3 = 2/3 L', 'lambda_4 = 2/4 L'
General expression at lower right: 'lambda_n = 2/n L' with 'n = 1, 2, 3, . . .'
Optional highlight annotations: node markers and antinode markers on the selected mode

interactions.label: Mode number n
interactions.teaches: Each successive mode packs one more half-wavelength into the same fixed length, adding one interior node and shortening the wavelength to 2L/n.

interactions.label: Play string oscillation
interactions.teaches: The pale and dark curves are the same string at opposite phases: nodes never move while antinodes swing through the full envelope.

interactions.label: String length L
interactions.teaches: Wavelength scales directly with string length at fixed n, so lambda_n = 2L/n holds for any string.

demo_steps.title: The fixed string
demo_steps.narration: A string of length L is clamped at both ends; those clamped points can never move, so they are permanent nodes. Every allowed wave must start and end at zero displacement.

demo_steps.title: Fundamental: one half-wavelength
demo_steps.narration: The simplest fit is a single hump with no interior nodes: exactly half a wavelength spans L, so 1/2 lambda_1 = L and lambda_1 = 2L.

demo_steps.title: Watch it vibrate
demo_steps.narration: Playing the motion shows the string sweeping between the dark and pale curves. The endpoints stay pinned while the centre antinode moves the most.

demo_steps.title: Second harmonic
demo_steps.narration: Fit two half-wavelengths and a node appears at the midpoint. Now lambda_2 = L — half the fundamental wavelength on the same string.

demo_steps.title: Third and fourth harmonics
demo_steps.narration: Three and then four half-wavelengths fit, giving two and three interior nodes and wavelengths 2L/3 and 2L/4. Only whole numbers of half-wavelengths are permitted.

demo_steps.title: Stretch the string
demo_steps.narration: Dragging L longer stretches every mode's wavelength in proportion while the number of nodes stays fixed, confirming lambda_n = 2L/n.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Boundary conditions quantize the wave: because both ends must be nodes, only wavelengths that fit a whole number of half-waves into L survive, so lambda_n = 2L/n.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Vertical stack of five panels on a white background, all sharing the same horizontal span. Top panel: a plain straight line between two small filled black dots labeled 'Node' below each end, with a thin double-headed arrow above it terminated by short vertical ticks and labeled 'L' at its centre. Below it, four evenly spaced wave panels labeled at the far left in italic serif as n = 1 through n = 4. Each panel shows a medium-dark steel-blue sinusoid and its light pale-blue mirror image, together forming a lens/envelope shape; both curves are pinned to black dots at the two ends, and they cross at n-1 interior points. Amplitude is the same for all modes. To the right of each panel, two math expressions in serif type, spaced apart: the fit condition (1/2 lambda_1 = L, lambda_2 = L, 3/2 lambda_3 = L, 4/2 lambda_4 = L) and the wavelength result (lambda_n = 2/n L form). Lower right of the whole figure carries the general rule lambda_n = 2/n L with n = 1, 2, 3, . . . . In the interactive version, the currently selected mode panel is highlighted (others dimmed), animated by interpolating the dark curve between the two envelopes with a sine-in-time factor, with small hollow circles marking nodes and small arrows or brackets marking antinodes on the active mode; the shared line length rescales horizontally with the L slider and the L dimension arrow rescales with it.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Button/state for mode number: the learner steps through n = 1, 2, 3, and 4, the standing-wave shape, interior nodes, and wavelength equation update, making clear that exactly n half-wavelengths must fit inside length L.
- Animation for the selected mode: the learner presses play for any mode, the string oscillates between the two envelope curves while endpoint and interior nodes stay fixed, making clear the difference between nodes and antinodes.
- Slider for string length L: the learner drags the endpoint separation, the displayed wavelength for the selected mode stretches or contracts with the string, making clear the relationship lambda_n = 2L/n.

authoredContext:
The lab setup shows a string attached to a string vibrator, which oscillates the string with an adjustable frequency f. The other end of the string passes over a frictionless pulley and is tied to a hanging mass. The magnitude of the tension in the string is equal to the weight of the hanging mass. The string has a constant linear density (mass per length) μ and the speed at which a wave travels down the string equals v=FTμ=mgμ another section. The symmetrical boundary conditions (a node at each end) dictate the possible frequencies that can excite standing waves. Starting from a frequency of zero and slowly increasing the frequency, the first mode n=1 appears as shown in the figure. The first mode, also called the fundamental mode or the first harmonic, shows half of a wavelength has formed, so the wavelength is equal to twice the length between the nodes λ1=2L. The fundamental frequency, or first harmonic frequency, that drives this mode is

The standing wave patterns that are possible for a string, the first four of which are shown in the figure, are known as the normal modes, with frequencies known as the normal frequencies. In summary, the first frequency to produce a normal mode is called the fundamental frequency (or first harmonic). Any frequencies above the fundamental frequency are overtones. The second frequency of the n=2 normal mode of the string is the first overtone (or second harmonic). The frequency of the n=3 normal mode is the second overtone (or third harmonic) and so on.

Standing waves created on a string of length L. A node occurs at each end of the string. The nodes are boundary conditions that limit the possible frequencies that excite standing waves. (Note that the amplitudes of the oscillations have been kept constant for visualization. The standing wave patterns possible on the string are known as the normal modes. Conducting this experiment in the lab would result in a decrease in amplitude as the frequency increases.)

Four figures of a string of length L are shown. Each has two waves. The first one has 1 node. It is labeled half lambda 1 = L, lambda 1 = 2 by 1 times L. The second figure has 2 nodes. It is labeled lambda 2 = L, lambda 2 = 2 by 2 times L. The third figure has three nodes. It is labeled 3 by 2 times lambda 3 = L, lambda 3 = 2 by 3 times L. The fourth figure has 4 nodes. It is labeled 4 by 2 times lambda 4 = L, lambda 4 = 2 by 4 times L. There is a derived formula at the bottom, lambda n equal to 2 by n times L for n = 1, 2, 3 and so on.

The next two modes, or the third and fourth harmonics, have wavelengths of λ3=23L and λ4=24L, driven by frequencies of f3=3v2L=3f1 and f4=4v2L=4f1. All frequencies above the frequency f1 are known as the overtones. The equations for the wavelength and the frequency can be summarized as:

discrepancies: Math typesetting is slightly off: λ subscripts sit well below the baseline and fraction denominators (the '2' in ½, the 'n' in 2/n) are dropped low relative to the numerator, so the stacked fractions read less cleanly than the crisp typeset fractions in the source.
The 'Play string oscillation' checkbox in the control panel is detached from its caption (floats above/right of the text), making that control ambiguous.
'n = 1, 2, 3, . . .' is rendered fully italic including the digits, whereas the source italicizes only the variable n.
The overall drawing is rendered slightly smaller/narrower than the source relative to the frame because of the side panel, making the small equation text near the limit of comfortable inline reading.
evaluation.notes: A very faithful reproduction of the four-harmonic standing-wave figure — correct dark/pale curve pairs, node dots, L dimension arrow, per-mode equations and the general λₙ = 2L/n rule — supported by rich, pedagogically apt interactions (mode buttons, L slider, oscillation animation, 6-step demo); main weaknesses are minor math-typesetting baseline issues and a misaligned checkbox control.

feedback.rationale: No failure modes or action items remain and all core scores are high; only minor cosmetic typesetting and alignment nits persist, so further iteration isn't warranted.
